Utilizing $6.0\, {\rm years}$ of data collected by the LHC and analyzed by the CMS collaboration, the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay process was studied to calculate the $\Gamma(B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-)$ value. By determining the $m(B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-)$ and $q(B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-)$ parameters from two million selected $K^+K^-$ pairs, corrections were made to account for limited particle momentum measurement and for $B^0_s$ mixing. Ultimately, the average particle lifetime was determined as $c\tau (B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-))=294.9\, {\rm \mu m}$, which represents an improvement in precision by a factor of two compared to the existing measurements used in the $B^0_s$ mixing calculation.

This research focuses on the numerical analysis of a discrete approximation method for a novel, probabilistically defined norm in a context of network stabilization. The underlying problem involves determining an optimal way to distribute power among a set of interconnected nodes, where the interconnections form a tree structure. The specific norm in question is defined in a probabilistic manner, resulting in the examination of the asymptotic behavior of this norm under certain conditions. The study establishes that the relevant constant has the same dimension as the square of a harmonic function, which has implications for the stability of the node network. The application of this constant to distributed issues highlights the necessity for further investigation into its properties, including the development of both direct and reverse estimation techniques, which in turn, facilitates a distributed algorithm for calculating this constant efficiently across the network without compromising its accuracy.

Given that the sky viewed by this detector covers only a small fraction of the sphere, the origin of these anomalies remains unclear, as they observed a limited portion of the particle sources over a brief duration.

This research focuses on identifying and resolving inconsistencies in database tables, particularly those containing null values and functional dependencies. We developed a new approach that uses generalized dependencies to handle inconsistencies arising from null values. Our method involves applying a new set of rules called null implications, which can be combined with existing dependency management techniques. We created a new, explicit format for expressing these rules and proposed a new, abstract graph structure to automatically derive them from existing dependencies. We developed a set of rules to transform these graph structures and created a prototype system to demonstrate our approach. We also established new, revised versions of well-known dependency properties that hold for all data within a table, even when values are missing. Our work contributes new tools and methods for maintaining data integrity and has broader implications for other information management tasks that deal with missing values.

This research introduces a dynamic statistical model named the Time Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TPAR) to address the limitations of the conventional Poisson Autoregressive (PAR) and Generalized Poisson Negative Binomial (GPNB) models.  TPAR combines the strengths of PAR and GPNB, providing a more flexible and generalized approach to analyzing count data with varying levels of dependence and dispersion.  A Bayesian estimation method utilizing the stochastic variable transformation and No-U-turn sampler techniques is developed to obtain the TPAR's posterior distribution.  Moreover, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach is employed to derive Bayesian estimates for the TPAR model's parameters.  A simulation study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian TPAR model estimation method.  Additionally, real-world data from the New York City 911 call system is analyzed using a Bayesian TPAR model, comparing the results with those obtained from a conventional PAR model and a Bayesian GPNB model.  Evaluation metrics including the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC), the Wide Information Criterion (WIC), and the Bayesian p-factor are employed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian TPAR model estimation method. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) for representing objects, which are fully differentiable and possess invariance to transformations under the special Euclidean group SE(3). Object-point clouds are input to the model, and the output is an 11-dimensional tensor that encapsulates the spatial relationship between query and source points in an equivariant manner, ensuring it adapts to object transformations under the special Euclidean group when points are translated, scaled, rotated, or translated in 3D space. We then apply this approach to object manipulation tasks, specifically using a policy gradient method with a vision encoder to predict end-effector actions based on object features, successfully learning policies for novel objects in simulation with a generalization capability to unseen objects. Our code and model are available at the provided GitHub repository link.

Researchers have developed a robust 'ladder' technique to calculate the precise location of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in classical systems exhibiting various universality classes. The results obtained through this method, when ladder TQFT is used to determine higher-order corrections, show a consistent match with the data derived from Monte Carlo simulations, confirming the validity of the ladder technique even in cases where it was previously thought incorrect. Notably, the calculated edge singularities for classical systems with varying N values fall within a distinct 10% width, contradicting the earlier 3/5 power-law growth prediction that suggested they should occur at identical times. The accuracy of this calculation further enables the determination of various critical exponents related to these edge singularities, including new insights into the characteristics of the systems in question.

In statistics and machine learning, the challenge of denoising high-dimensional Gaussian signals is addressed using the TAP algorithm, and our research reveals an anomaalous behavior near a critical noise threshold through an investigation of the TAP free energy's local concavity. As this free energy exhibits concavity in a small range, a corresponding change in the TAP algorithm's stability is observed, algorithmically shifting from contraction to expansion precisely at the identified threshold. Moreover, our findings allow for a broader, locally valid adjustment of the TAP algorithm to restore contraction and enhance signal recovery, even beyond the high-temperature regime. Additionally, we develop a localized version of the Sudakov-Fernique lemma that yields the TAP free energy's concavity, and which, when applied to a queue of transformations, results in the existence of a unique, non-trivial point of local minimization in the TAP landscape, thereby demonstrating the failure of the pure TAP algorithm's convergence and illustrating its lack of convexity.

The utilization of stellar photometry systems has been effective in monitoring changes in the atmosphere, including aerosols, for over half a century. Despite the limitation of these systems providing broad measurements with specific filters, they have been valuable in complementing detailed studies conducted with narrow-field spectroscopic systems and aerosol remote sensing instruments. Recent studies have reanalyzed data from all photometric systems with the addition of calibration standards, revealing improved assessments of the vertical distribution of aerosols compared to traditional methods. The revised analysis highlights revised analysis reveals comparable lower and upper limits estimated using spectroscopic and remote sensing systems and expands our understanding of the frequency of near-lower and upper limits through probability distributions derived from spectroscopic and remote sensing systems. This has significant implications for revising current assessment averages and underscores the reliability of photometric systems with appropriate calibration standards for detailed studies involving the analysis of aerosols in the atmosphere.

Accurate 6D pose estimation of objects in unstructured environments poses a significant challenge due to the vast search space and the intricate relationship between object pose and pixel-level patterns. To effectively tackle this challenge, we focus on two critical areas of research: leveraging the structural knowledge of projection groups and incorporating semantic information to enhance correspondence learning. Specifically, we integrate a two-stream network that leverages local features of objects to identify the relationships between objects' visible surfaces and their hidden faces, and objects' orientations to their opposites. Following this, we search for the object's pose by evaluating the compatibility between the objects' visible surfaces and their faces/opposites in the scene. For robust performance, our method also incorporates data augmentation and a novel loss function, known as the hybrid correspondence learning loss, to efficiently train the network's regression module, called DeepHMap++. Extensive experiments conducted on the LINEMODE dataset demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of accuracy and reliability.

Python is a widely used tool in statistics and machine learning due to its
simplicity, extensive documentation, and vast array of pre-built tools that
significantly enhance productivity. GGLasso is a new Python module specifically
designed to facilitate a wide range of Generalized Graphical Lasso problems,
commonly encountered in Bayesian network structure learning, Bayesian network
structure reconstruction from known distributions, and precision matrix estimation.
Each assumption underlying a Bayesian network problem or a positive definite
solution corresponds to a distinct variant of the Generalized Graphical Lasso,
which has numerous applications and requires different algorithms to solve. GGLasso
achieves this versatility by utilizing Python's capability to handle generic
convex optimization problems through the Graphical Lasso as a side constraint,
implemented via the cvxpy module. GGLasso extends a previous Python implementation
by adding two additional Bayesian network structure learning variants and a known
data matrix option, while also providing a comprehensive set of tests to ensure
accurate and reliable computations. GGLasso is distinct from existing R modules
such as bgmlearn, network structure learning from probabilities, and network
structure learning from CP-structures in terms of its functionality and
implementation.

The equilibrium configuration of equilibrium polymeric and biological macromolecular systems can be significantly influenced by various constraints imposed on the system, including the addition of molecules, macrocyclic structures, and closed loops. Investigating the equilibrium configurations of these systems is crucial, yet it presents a significant computational challenge due to the intricate interplay of molecular dynamics and the complex configuration space. In this study, we investigate the robustness and efficiency of Langevin Dynamics in exploring the polymeric configuration space, even in the presence of constrained systems. Our results indicate that Langevin Dynamics is well-suited for exploring complex configurations, provided the time step used in the simulation is chosen carefully to ensure accurate results. Our research also demonstrates the applicability of this approach to systems with highly intricate constraints, including those with multiple loops or constrained molecules incorporated into the system.

We introduce the concept of reliant node prominence (RNP), drawing from a dynamic relationship between node-promotion vectors and residual information unexplained by prominent vectors. RNP is particularly suited for assessing entity distinctiveness in multi-dimensional network structures. We integrate RNP with eigenvector prominence (EP) methodology, under the assumption that prominent vectors represent the most distinct network information. This combination creates a new evaluation approach called eigenvector prominence for multilayer networks (EPMN). In the context of Type IIB theory with matter, we've identified a mechanism for maximizing the effect of (generalized) theta-terms after integrating out degrees of freedom. This involves the formation of a vacuum expectation value of a bi-linear scalar order parameter that breaks a U(1)^(4) global symmetry, potentially enhancing the (generalized) theta-terms to 3+1 dimension. We've developed a framework for analyzing this process using an effective field theory (EFT) with WZ terms, whose behavior is influenced by possible higher-dimensional operators. We've explored the conditions under which the (generalized) theta-terms can be maximally broken, which can unlock new (or reveal hidden) phenomena. Furthermore, we've established the relevance of our approach to various manifestations of (3+1)-dimensional (generalized) theta-terms arising from the Type IIB theory with matter, including stringy, Kaluza-Klein, and instanton contributions.

The chemical composition of quaternary compounds with two electron holes per atom shows a wide range of electrical properties, from conductors that separate charges to insulators due to repulsive electron forces. To understand how specific electron interactions affect these properties in quaternary compounds, this research focuses on cupricite, a compound with strong repulsive forces, and investigates its electronic structure. Using multiple methods, results indicate that this cupricite should be considered as an unconventional example of orbital-selective insulation, in which electrons in certain electron pathways lack sufficient repulsion to become localized and instead behave like an insulator, while those in other pathways are highly localized and contribute to overall resistance. This finding challenges traditional views of this compound and opens up new possibilities for using iron-based minerals as semiconducting materials.

The behavior of quantum systems under the influence of a driving force often exhibits rich and diverse dynamics, including a phenomenon known as Rabi oscillations. In the context of the spin-1 Dicke model without an external magnetic field, we investigate Rabi oscillations under various conditions, including those influenced by strong coupling effects and quantum fluctuations. Our research reveals the existence of a previously unobserved phenomenon - exceptionally large Rabi frequencies occurring at frequencies where the driving force's frequency is near zero, a condition we term "Rabi hollow oscillations." A numerical model demonstrates the feasibility of observing this phenomenon using a Yttrium Aluminum Perovskite doped with Europium as a material medium, where the extremely long lifetime of the excited state enables the realization of Rabi hollow oscillations as predicted by our study.

Utilizing a Hartree-Fock approach, we discovered that specific non-symmorphic lattices have adjustable band gaps and can move their Dirac points to various high-symmetry locations in reciprocal space. These effects are also visible in a simplified, non-stochastic triangular lattice made of helium atoms adsorbed on a silicon surface.

A new approach to identifying chemical formulas for polymers is presented, combining linear regression and integer optimization methods. This strategy treats the elements within a polymer as coefficients in a system of equations, which are derived from conservation laws for each element present in the polymer. The masses of these elements are obtained from spectroscopic analysis of the polymer, and additional constraints are applied to ensure the resulting formula adheres to chemical principles, such as those governing ionic bonding. This method is tested using chemical formulas for well-known polymers, including sodium sulfide glass ($Na_2O \cdot SiO_2$), Teflon ($CF_2$), Nylon 6,6 ($[C_{12}H_{22}N_2O_2]_x$), and polysaccharides like cellulose and starch ($[C_6H_{10}O_5]_x$). The proposed technique effectively reconstructs the chemical formulas for these polymers from the masses of their constituent elements.

The human esophagus, which connects the mouth to the stomach, is a narrow muscular tube. It's home to various types of tumors including stenosis, cancer, and diverticula, which can obstruct the esophagus and cause symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, chest pain, heartburn, and weight loss. A study was conducted to compare the effectiveness of manual segmentation and an automated method based on a modified 3D U-Net network in segmenting neoplasms in the esophagus from CT images. The original U-Net network was enhanced through several modifications including the incorporation of dense connections, attention mechanisms, and dilated convolutions to create a network called DDAUnet. Multiple modifications to the network's input and skip connections were tested and optimized for the best results in neoplasm segmentation. Experimental testing involved using the publicly available dataset from PubMed, comprising 50 images from five different patients, and the network achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.45 and a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.5 in neoplasm segmentation. Although the results indicated room for improvement, the study demonstrated the potential of the DDAUnet network in neoplasm segmentation in the esophagus.

Multilingual individuals commonly use a single language to convey multiple ideas, as they blend different languages into a unique form of communication that reflects their personal experiences and backgrounds. This communication style, known as code-switching or code-mixing, poses significant obstacles for traditional machine translation systems and text classification models trained on monolingual datasets, as they struggle to accurately interpret the mixed-language content without extensive, expensive parallel training data. Our examination of existing research and real-world applications reveals an inconsistent pattern in studies that don't explicitly address crucial factors such as world knowledge, world knowledge + character embeddings, and the balance between the first and second language components in code-mixing. Furthermore, we highlight the need for innovative, efficient evaluation methods and optimized mixed-language datasets to move beyond simply adapting current monolingual models through domain randomization. We also explore potential research directions and promising avenues for developing more effective tools to serve multilingual communities.

As multiple human evaluation methods for improved digital systems are recognized, we investigate utilizing human feedback on image description generators. We analyze presenting potential descriptions to raters alongside reference text, and without it, in RCTs, two studies with 86 and 160 participants for 200 images each demonstrate that showing reference text improves Rater accuracy by 7.5%. However, when reference text is covertly supplied, improving Rater performance by the same margin, descriptions alone have no adverse effect on their results. Based on these findings, we recommend incorporating Rater performance benchmarks with corresponding reference text to verify the validity of quality assessments for automated improvements.

Through the use of multiple methodologies and methodologies, including the Gaussian Approximation Method and Grand Canonical Monte Carlo Simulations, researchers were able to determine a unique, symmetric crystal structure for Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its most stable state. By analyzing Ta$_2$O$_5$'s properties and investigating a range of possible crystal structures, the current study discovered that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has an unusually low coordination number of 4 and exhibits semiconducting properties with an indirect band gap of 2.4eV. The results indicate that the Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structure exhibits extreme anharmonicity and that the existing Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structures are actually oxidized forms of the Ta$_2$O$_4$ structure. The current study also identified four additional Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structures with varying semiconducting properties and coordinated oxide geometries.

Previous studies on the `big_data.sort.by.geography` feature of Reddit have examined its use without considering whether geographic information was accurate or its source. This research specifically investigates the geographic sorting feature of major U.S. cities, including Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York City on Reddit. Our study employed a combination of descriptive and experimental methods to analyze whether this geographic sorted subreddits were effective tools for spreading both factual and misleading news. Our findings revealed that geographic sorted subreddits are frequently utilized as platforms for spreading both factual and deceptive content, with a 19% higher influence than a 15% increase in the false news experiment, as measured by the likelihood of sharing false statements. Overall, our results offer valuable insights into how large-scale, geographically based data can be utilized and also highlight the necessity of accounting for data inaccuracies in computational social science investigations.

Verbal guidance from human instructors plays a significant role in learning, yet the specific linguistic features that facilitate effective learning have been underexplored in research focusing on manipulation tasks and robot interaction. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by systematically analyzing spoken instructions from humans demonstrating tasks to robots. Human instructors demonstrated a simple task involving the placement of an object into a container with container volume information provided verbally, either generally or specifically, to a robot equipped with speech recognition capabilities. Through computational analysis, distinct patterns were identified in the structure and acoustic characteristics of instructions, revealing that the spoken instructions were not uniform but rather varied significantly. These findings have valuable implications for both human learning when observing tasks and for developing more effective robot learning systems that utilize verbal instructions.

A novel approach to understanding the intricate behavior of 2D turbulent flows has been discovered by linking the Euler equations to complex structures known as conformal field theories. This study builds upon a previous theory, establishing a direct correspondence where the degrees of complexity in these theories mirror one another. A meaningful example was examined where the theoretical complexity was calculated using both predictions, revealing a precise match in both c-values of 1/24.

The evaluation of machine components that engage in conversations with humans is a pressing issue. Repeating traditional testing methods, like those based on Berkeley NLP frameworks, isn't effective for machines that utilize deep learning technologies, which depend on vast amounts of data for their performance. Requiring human annotators to repeat assessments is both time-consuming and costly. Our proposed solution, machine-generated examination papers, is a new testing framework tailored for conversational machines utilizing deep learning technologies. This system utilizes the underlying structure of machine components as a reference, utilizing a typical set of inputs to evaluate their outputs, which can be efficiently updated using various techniques. The system is designed to be cost-effective and rapid in creation. We demonstrated the efficiency of machine-generated examination papers by comparing different R BERT models' capabilities in the TREC conversational track 2020, showing a 0.2 increase in CDM scores and a 0.05 increase in user satisfaction surveys when used in evaluation processes.

Due to the widespread adoption of digital devices and the abundance of online content, users are increasingly confronted with an overwhelming number of recommendations across multiple, disjointed platforms.  In order to improve the effectiveness and personalization of recommendation systems, particularly in reducing sparse data issues and enhancing the diversity of recommended domains, this research introduces a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSD-CR).  The proposed framework incorporates an innovative domain knowledge graph that integrates diverse, sparse domains and cross-domain embedding layers to effectively transfer useful information between domains.  Furthermore, MSD-CR includes a unique multi-task learning module to explore diverse user preferences across different domains, resulting in a more thorough and personalized understanding of user preferences.  The proposed method is evaluated using three real-world datasets and shows superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of recommendation accuracy and domain diversity.

The investigation of the feasibility of implementing a desired conic structure in a given delivery set is referred to as the natural conic expression problem (NXP). This paper introduces the use of BarrierKernel.jl and Hypatia.jl to effectively solve NXPs belonging to leading modern conic families. We achieve this by formulating NXP problems as pairs of primal-dual barrierless Newton forms, specifically designed to maintain the natural domains of their associated modern conic structures. This approach enables us to successfully solve NXP problems for Hergert's novel conic extension, as well as for other prominent conic families such as semidefinite, copositive, and hypelliptic cones. We illustrate this process by providing actual working code and visualizations of NXP solutions for these conic families.

Recent advances in medical image analysis have relied heavily on deep learning, and there have been various proposed quality assurance methods that have achieved impressive performance. However, our research reveals that many of these results may be overoptimistic and suffer from generalization issues caused by data testing and training sets being incorrectly mixed. We found that this problem arises in prominent publications and widely used datasets, and it leads to results that are both performance inflations and generalization issues. We demonstrate this with rigorous, reproducible experiments involving ten published methods and seven datasets. We propose and examine seven different scenarios that incorporate a more robust evaluation and generalization capability. Our experiments indicate that nine out of ten published methods lead to inflated results and generalize poorly. We discovered that even popular methods, including those employed in leading institutions and published venues, lead to results that are both inflated and suffer from generalization issues caused by this common and confusing practice. We propose and examine multiple scenarios leading to results that are both accurate and generalizable, which should serve as a standard for the community.

This research investigates how private electric car ownership impacts the ability of distribution networks to recover from disruptions. Recognizing that grid outages can significantly delay charging and increase recharging costs, and that this psychological and financial burden varies among consumers, we modeled the relationship between preparedness and outages using a power and electric vehicle loss function. Preparedness, in our analysis, included the choice of battery capacity and the level of self-sufficiency achieved through on-site generators. Furthermore, we employed a novel multi-agent optimization framework to analyze preparedness decisions in the context of grid failures, and used game theory to pinpoint conditions under preparedness becomes a dominant strategy for all players, thereby minimizing the economic and psychological losses associated with grid outages.

In this work, we explore the challenges of a solitary encounter between two individuals who are motivated by incentive and tend to repeat the same action. While previous research has focused primarily on single-agent scenarios, we address the complexity of such meetings from a multi-agent perspective. A key aspect of this study involves agents with memory, where we utilize a recurrent neural network modeled after working memory. Our approach is evaluated using two setups: simultaneous decision-making and sequential actions. Notably, in the simultaneous scenario where agents make decisions at the same time, we discover a single strategy that can lead to a repeated encounter. In the sequential setup, we observe two distinct strategies that can result in a repeated meeting. Our study yields valuable insights into the action spaces required for a solitary encounter, providing implications for understanding the solitary behavior in multi-agent environments.

This research utilizes an ab initio approach to examine the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 for x = 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75. Using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method, we examined these materials under experimental and body-centered tetragonal structures in order to determine their ground state configurations and explain their observed behavior. The results revealed that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit indirect band gaps along specific crystallographic directions and that the rare earth 4f electrons in these materials are localized within narrow bands near the Fermi level, contributing to ferromagnetic behavior consistent with the Stoner criterion. Furthermore, Gd0.5Cm0.5Sn3 exhibits a direct band gap in the antiferromagnetic configuration, while the remaining materials display indirect band gaps and specific directions for electron and hole mobility. The calculated densities of states and projected densities of states provide a comprehensive explanation for the materials' ferromagnetic behavior.

The Big Bang theory predicts the universe should consist primarily of photons, with a smaller proportion of baryons and mesons made up of quarks. However, observations of the universe's actual content show a near-complete lack of these baryonic substances. This discrepancy suggests that roughly 85% of the universe's baryons must be hidden from our detection methods. We propose three theories to account for this "dark baryon" phenomenon. Firstly, we suggest that these baryons could be concealed within the super-heavy axion-isoscalar bosons, potentially reaching a minimum mass of around 4.2 Mev and a maximum mass of approximately 10^37 kg. Secondly, we propose that the baryons might be trapped in the ultra-dense, non-relativistic meson gas that could exist around the Planck temperature of roughly 10^32 K. Lastly, we offer a third explanation rooted in the general theory of relativity.

For any finite dimensional real vector space V, there exists a compact subset W within the group GL(V)'s compact-open topology that exhibits the following four characteristics: it serves as the smallest closed and covariant subset containing the set of all elementary matrices, also known as elementary generators; it has a finite number of distinct left-cosads under the GL(V) action; it has a finite number of distinct right-cosads under the GL(V) action; and it has a finite number of distinct cosads under the GL(V) action. This set W is referred to as the geometric structure of the group GL(V). If the vector space V possesses a non-trivial set of linearly independent vectors that are both orthogonal and normalized, referred to as a Coxeter system, then we denote the group of transformations preserving the orientation and acting on these vectors as the B-type Coxeter group, den as WB. It has been proven that the geometric structure of the group Coxeter WB can be determined by examining a subset of GL(V) that also exhibits the four initial characteristics, referred to as W'B, which can be obtained from WB by removing a specific number of elements den as (n+1)(n+2)/2. Moreover, a distinct geometric structure can be established for the W'B that does not rely on the choice of the Coxeter system, den as W'.

Cosmological studies based on Type Ia Supernovae (SNIa) data have been influenced by gravitational lensing, which provides constraints on dark matter and influences the interpretation of CPla observations. A key challenge in understanding lensing effects on SNIa involves accounting for the distribution of matter on both large and small scales. Researchers have previously employed gravitational lensing effects on distant SNIa to derive limits on the properties of dark matter, but such analyses are complicated by the limited sensitivity of SNIa observations to the gravitational environments in which they occur, particularly for marginally lensed events. A new investigation examined the lensing effects on the observed brightness of 547 P50-deconvolved SNIa from the Pantheon sample, by employing an advanced method to identify lensed events through cross-correlation with LIGO/Virgo gravitational wave observations of binary neutron star mergers, but found that highly lensed events are rare and most observed SNIa occur with negligible lensing effects, providing an overall multiplicative factor of $1.02 \pm 0.04$ in the distance modulus of the Pantheon sample, which needs to be adjusted in precise cosmological analyses incorporating gravitational lensing effects on SNIa.

T-shaped waveguide junctions, referred to as T hubs, are an essential component in integrated photonics.  We have developed an integrated training framework for T hubs based on Maxwell's equations, featuring T-shaped waveguide junctions with bending elements and balanced transmission paths.  Our approach includes an automated simulation method that ensures the straight arm of the T hub transfers 90% of the input signal to both output bends with equal intensity.  This integrated training method results in high-accuracy designs for T hubs with straight and curved components, achieving 99.6% transmission at 1550 nm with a 30 dB bandwidth of 100 nm.  Our design also achieves a compact footprint of 150 um x 150 um and demonstrates consistent and transferable performance across different geometries and silicon thicknesses.

The use of prior knowledge about the context in which a target is located has significantly enhanced the performance of traditional object recognition systems. The introduction of the Deep Context Object Recognizer (DCOR) knows the spatial arrangement of objects in an image, enabling it to detect solitary objects within images and scenes within images. Our research analysis reveals that the incorporation of contextual information is highly beneficial for the majority of DCOR's applications, particularly in the object detection dataset Cityscapes Object. To quantify the impact of prior knowledge, we employed the concept of context from previous research and modified DCOR by replacing its current feature set with a simpler point in space representation. Our experimental results indicate that the current DCOR context prior effectively contributes to the performance of DCOR, primarily by preventing the overconfidence of the deep object recognizers in cases where the target may not actually be present.

Differential operators on complex symplectic manifolds can be transformed into a new symplectic structure through multiplication and the conjugation operator, altering the underlying symplectic form of the manifold. This paper explores the relationship between these differential operators and the resulting changes to the symplectic structure, providing a criterion to determine when such transformations lead to isomorphism with the original manifold and its new associated structure. A comparison is also made between this differential-induced alteration and another type of alteration studied by Nagami. The concept of symplectic resistance is introduced as a measure of the difficulty in establishing such an isomorphism, and it's shown that this resistance for $\mathbb{C}^2$ is equivalent to a function previously defined by Le and Scherer.

There is no clear indication of what constitutes a compatible or incompatible kidney for a patient waiting for a transplant, nor is there an accepted ideal kidney transplant candidate. Using data from the 2013 US transplant system, we analyzed 24,489 adult kidney transplants to determine the characteristics of the ideal kidney donor and recipient. We found that the ideal donor would be female, around 34 years old, of white race, with no diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, or obesity. The ideal recipient would be male, around 44 years old, with native disease, and a history of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, heart failure, heart transplants, liver transplants, liver failure, heart-liver transplants, heart-liver failure transplants, and liver failure transplants, and would undergo up to three transplants, with the current wait time being approximately 3.3 years. Our findings are based on the US transplant system in 2013 and may not apply to other countries or time periods. They highlight the importance of broadening the kidney donor pool, particularly by considering older, non-white donors with comorbidities, and with the support of policies promoting equitable access to transplants for marginalized communities.

We investigate the mechanisms by which deep learning models, specifically a CTRM-based neural network, embody the Loughran-McDonald sentiment scale. Our analysis involves extracting individual words from financial texts and associating them with high-dimensional spaces that capture their emotional connotations. Subsequent visualization techniques, including principal component analysis and non-linear dimensionality reduction, are employed to create a graphical representation of the network's comprehension of each word in relation to the sentiment scale. Our comprehensive evaluation manually verifies the emotional orientation of 400 words and reveals that the network generally encodes positive and negative sentiments in an opposing manner, aligned with the Loughran-McDonald sentiment scale. Our research also identifies instances of words with ambiguous emotional connotations and difficult-to-categorize neutral words. The manual analysis of associated word representations demonstrates that contextual information can significantly influence the emotional connotation of certain words and that the majority of company-related words possess both positive and negative dimensions. Our paper provides a detailed exploration of the emotional connotations of frequently occurring words in financial texts and potentially bridges the methodological approaches used to encode sentiment within deep learning models.

This work provides the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM algorithms that mirror the extra energy gained from using multiple antennas and multiple frequencies in integrated energy and information transfer (IBIT). In previous research, a novel waveform was created in IBIT that uses multiple frequencies and multiple antennas, from which information data could be transmitted using conventional OFDM technology while additional energy harvest could be gained by IBIT receivers with suitable hardware. In this paper, we examine the possibility of achieving the same level of additional energy harvest in IBIT with OFDM signals transmitted from a single antenna and from multiple antennas, respectively. We then concentrate on maximizing the additional energy harvest in these two cases by modifying the OFDM waveforms, without affecting the information data transmitted. Numerical results in this paper are based on numerical experiments with mixed OFDM data and energy transmission (IEBT).

We investigate learning outcomes that fall within the framework of rationalizability in multiplayer games featuring continuously changing rewards. By employing the projective equilibrium policy in multiple rounds, we prove that various popular learning algorithms can achieve outcomes that are both rationalizable and equilibrium outcomes that are stable under rationalizability. Furthermore, by utilizing the UCBEQ policy in a two-player setting with smooth reward functions, we obtain the first learning result achieving outcomes that are rationalizable for all games, obtaining the first outcome that is equilibrium under rationalizability when the payoffs are known, and obtaining the first outcome that is equilibrium under rationalizability in a zero-sum game. Our main achievement is quantifying the rate of convergence in terms of the number of repetitions required to reach outcomes that are both stable and rationalizable in learning scenarios, all of which were previously unattained.

In our analysis of conversation scenarios, we've broken down the complexity of human dialogue into a step-by-step process, considering factors such as hyphotheses, discussions with experts, and discussions with laypeople. We've designed a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 10,000 transcripts from 650 unique situations, where each situation can branch into multiple paths through different concepts and discussions with experts and laypeople. The properties of our data and the design of the MultiTalk test suite, which includes assessments for hearing and language problems, are outlined in our paper, where we provide examples of our approach and propose a new framework for evaluating the durability of conversational agents in real-world settings.

We developed a novel approach to expedite N-body simulations for generalized gravity theories by modifying a well-established, rapidly executed baseline gravity simulation. In this altered framework, a specific gravitational model is introduced via the adjustment of a diagonal component in the matter field's energy-momentum tensor. By decoupling this adjustment from the simulation process, we can utilize existing, highly efficient N-body baseline simulations to generate data for a wide range of algorithms and parameters related to these generalized models. For cosmological applications involving multiple species, each species' distribution can be determined by running the corresponding baseline simulation and applying the necessary rescaling and transformation to retrieve the desired outcome. This approach allows us to bypass the computationally expensive general relativistic iterations typically required in previous simulations. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by utilizing 414 past baseline simulations (lasting less than one second each) to create 41,800 simulations for a particular model (BIGANG) in a wide parameter space.

We establish that the independence of disjoint chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) paths can be characterized through the Gaussian free field (GFQ) without relying on the conformal invariance property, by using the GFQ to define a family of disjoint SLE paths in a local time manner and proving their independence and distribution match those of a multiple SLE process.

WorkingWiki is an open-access, collective research tool built on the MediaWiki framework that enables collaborative editing and browsing for scholarly work. We introduced WorkingWiki as an accessible, transparent alternative to closed-access alternatives like preprints. By making all changes to content traceable to specific users and by allowing other users to reverse changes, WorkingWiki fosters accountability and transparency. We demonstrated the accountability and transparency of collective editing on Three Ways, a section of the WorkingWiki that we collaborated on with input from other users. By facilitating accessible, transparent, and accountable research collaboration, we argue that platforms like the WorkingWiki can be beneficial for a wide range of applications.

The reaction of a turbulent jet flame to sound waves is generally considered too complex to be inherently unstable or explosive, yet real-world examples suggest many jet fires behave unpredictably and release enormous energy. Using high-speed video footage, we monitored the fluctuations in the base diameter of a 100mm jet fire fueled by methane and releasing around 20MW of power, suspended above the ground. By measuring the periodic changes in flame length and base diameter, we determined the reaction of the flame to sound, along with its own potential source of energy. Furthermore, in a computer model, we replicated the flame's response to sound using mathematical simulations and an innovative technique known as the Active Flame Method, revealing that the flame can act as both a driver and driver modulator of pipe vibrations, leading to catastrophic failures in jet fire scenarios.

We used the neutrino mass ordering as the primary constraint in our study, supplemented by neutrinoless double beta decay measurements from three experiments and theoretical limits on its half-life. Additionally, we took into account the precise results from the PLANCK collaboration on the universe's neutrino cosmology to gain more accurate estimates of the interaction between ultralight dark matter and neutrinos. Using a Bayesian approach and specific dark matter parameters, we determined that the lightest neutrino mass is approximately $0.0024$ eV to $0.0038$ eV with a 68% confidence interval. These estimates varied depending on specific dark matter parameters, and we found that for some parameters, the lightest neutrino mass range was between $0.0065$ eV and $0.0098$ eV, while for others, it was between $0.0021$ eV and $0.0032$ eV, all within a 68% confidence interval. Our analysis also showed that the neutrino mass ordering could be neutrino-normal or neutrino-inverted, and we found that the neutrino mass values were influenced by the specific dark matter parameters and the results of the neutrinoless double beta decay experiments.

Nonlocal gravity theories introduce modifications to the Einstein-Hilbert action by adding a nonlocal curvature term, which is defined through a "constitutive connection" that must share specific characteristics with the Levi-Civita connection, including being metric-compatible and unimodular. By integrating these connections into the action and applying specific transformations, we can rephrase nonlocal gravity theories in a formal "essential tetrad" gravity framework. This rephrasing enables us to calculate key parameters, such as the constitutive connection, from observed data, using an analogy to "inverse problem" solutions in conventional essential tetrad theories. In this context, specific nonlocal gravity models can be solved and compared to a "standard model" created from a minimal nonlocal term, revealing insights into the complexity of these models in relation to the minimal nonlocal term.

Understanding the genetic basis of complex human traits has been significantly advanced through large-scale efforts to map remaining uncharacterized genes and consolidate association data from genome-wide studies. By combining results from these two types of analyses, researchers found that genes linked to various traits, including metabolism, cardiovascular health, cancer development, behavior, and immune function, tend to exhibit specific functional characteristics. When examining associations between genes and traits statistically, patterns became apparent across multiple studies with over 80 genes showing divergent expression levels in relation to a wide array of human characteristics.

This thesis explores the physics potential of rare particle collisions and investigates key areas where interest in rare collisions is rising, including vector boson scattering, boson tagging, and vector boson production through vector boson fusion. Studies were also conducted on rare processes involving bottom quarks produced in association with vector bosons or Higgs bosons, as well as rare processes like same-sign WW scattering. A analysis of rare collisions with proton-electron collisions was undertaken, focusing on the production of W bosos in association with an electron or photon in the final state. Finally, studies were done on rare processes like vector boson scattering in e-p collisions and the associated production of a bottom quark and a W bosos with photon tagging.

The recurrence intervals of X-ray binary transients in the Milky Way's centre display varying durations from months to years. Based on recent observations of Sgr A*'s transient events and our new analysis of past transient events in the Milky Way's centre, we found that their recurrence periods fluctuate significantly. This finding contradicts the prediction made by the stellar migration model proposed by Gurovich et al., which suggests a direct correlation between the migration times of star-forming clusters and the timing of transient events. We found that the migration times of these clusters do not correlate with their recurrence periods, as indicated by our statistical assessment. As a result, most of these clusters likely contain massive direct-collapse black holes that were formed recently in the clusters, as indicated by mass function measurements and the absence of neutron stars. As a result, the recurrence of transient events in these quiescent X-ray binaries depends on the presence and distribution of massive black holes and the velocity of their movement through a dense cluster of stars.

Based on a comprehensive, ab initio simulation, we identify and analyze the coupled spin-vibration and electron-phonon inertia forces arising from the acceleration of atomic electrons and atomic nuclei during their relative movement and subsequent deceleration. These coupled forces are found to be consistently present and influence the magnitude and frequency of the overall vibration-induced effect. The typical magnitude of these forces is in the range of micro-electron volts per angstrom, with their influence more pronounced in molecules than in crystalline solids. To effectively account for these forces, new, more elevated scaling laws must be applied, with possible adjustments needed in various applications, including frequency modulation in molecules for electron spin resonance in isotopes, and slight modifications in solids may have minimal effects. To demonstrate this, relevant theoretical equations, demonstration models, and relevant experimental proposals have been included.

We've developed a new approach to computationally simulating rotating objects beyond the restrictive assumption of uniform mass distribution used in traditional analytical models. By employing a full hydrodynamical modeling method with SPH, we can accurately capture both the shape and mass distribution of rotating objects, including stars and substellar bodies. Our simulations consider a rotating object with 0.35 times the mass of Jupiter, simulating the effects of rotation at various masses, spins, and equations of state. We found that the object can be stably rotated without material loss up to shedding points that vary depending on the equation of state, rotating object's spin, and mass. Our modeling shows the objects can be significantly flattened due to rotation with maximum flattening amounts of approximately 25% just before shedding occurs. We found that our results closely matched previous modeling and analytical results for low-rotating objects but differed for objects with high levels of rotation. We found the most accurate approximation of shedding point occurs in objects with a rate of rotation close to Kepler's orbit frequency at the object's surface, but this point does not necessarily coincide with the point of mass loss.

A distinctive hypothesis is proposed to explain the remnant detection of high-energy particle streams based on the total observed afterglow energy. According to our novel "universal afterglorgram" concept, which is primarily dependent on time and a star-forming region's particle density, each afterglow serves as an indicator of its surrounding environment's long-term energy distribution. A statistical approach is applied to the Chinese Wide-field Survey Afterglor data set, integrating the proposed dynamic afterglow model and its environment distribution, resulting in 12 detected streams considered potential particle stream remnant candidates. A second, independent energy distribution analysis is then applied to explain the energy of the 12 detected afterglows, which is found to be consistent with previous research on afterglow and star-forming region research.

This research focuses on developing a new, more efficient and robust propulsion system for pneumatic legged robots. As legs become increasingly complex and capable, they also present greater challenges in terms of being compact, efficient and physically sturdy. After reviewing various propulsion methods, we propose a novel, hybrid system that combines gas-driven actuators with a propeller-based propulsion mechanism for our newly designed TR-2 bipedal robot. This design is intended to overcome limitations of current pneumatic robots and enable them to tackle demanding tasks that were previously difficult. We anticipate gas-driven actuators to reach a point where they can handle heavy loads efficiently and allow for larger, more powerful robots. In contrast, conventional compressors that use electric motors present size and efficiency limitations. We propose a remote, solid-compressed air supply system designed to be both highly efficient and physically sturdy, employing thick walls to withstand high pressures and minimize leakage risks. We plan to put the proposed design and concept to the test with the TR-2 robot, initially on flat surfaces and subsequently on challenging terrains such as snow.

We establish sufficient conditions for a domain to be valued when the residue map is known to be surjective. Specifically, it's proven that if R is a valued domain, then the idealization of R over its nil radical is also valued. Additionally, the paper explores how various domain properties such as being a GCD domain, a Krull domain, or a completely integrally closed domain relate to being valued, in the context of R when R is a local domain. It's known that over the idealization of R, the concept of being a valued domain is equivalent to being a half-valued domain, but the known properties do not translate in the same way to the domain R itself. However, the paper provides characterization of valued domains with respect to various domain properties in the context of R when R is a local domain.

We introduce a novel knotting invariant for classical and welded links based on the number of crossings in a representation. This invariant, known as the minimal crossing number, allows us to establish inequalities, such as $c(\ell) \leq \sigma_{\ w}(\ell)$ for classical links, where $c(\ell)$ and $\sigma_{\ w}(\ell)$ denote the minimal crossing number and the Sterner–Wu invariant, respectively. Moreover, a minimal crossing reduction operator is defined for the welded knot module that preserves the relationship between the Jones and Kauffman states. However, this operator results in the unknotting of all classical knots and links, in stark contrast to other invariant-based operators which yield the unit without unwinding the knot or link structure. These findings lead to intriguing consequences, including the conclusion that any non-trivial classical knot can be unwound without passing the rope through each other or through the table, where the rope is ideally made of a fluid that can flow through each other and through the table, as long as the number of crossings of the resulting configuration is recorded.

In our study, a tactical collaborative framework for multiple agents is developed, focusing on overcoming communication limitations in a dynamic environment. The complexity issue is decomposed into two manageable parts: an optimized set of collaborative tactics is determined through simulation, and a component for managing limited resources is developed, enabling the execution of selected strategies within network constraints. The proposed tactical collaboration method is tested in a simulated scenario involving multiple agents navigating an enclosed space to locate and unlock locked doors within a specified timeframe.

This research delves into privacy concerns in a new application of Federated Learning known as Vertical Federated Learning. In this VFL setting, we identify two primary parties: one who manages the common features through aggregate training, and another who handles unique features during training, with sensitive personal data held locally by both parties on separate devices. The study first develops a pragmatic assault called a "Poisoning Prayer" that combines active and passive information gathering, posing a serious threat to data confidentiality. To counter this, a robust prevention method based on an inference model is proposed and an iterative training approach is developed for the Poission Prayer model to be deployed on both parties' systems. The proposed techniques were tested using real-world datasets for VFL training, and the results confirm that the Prayer Poising strategy outperforms random guessing with a 14.1% improvement, while the countermeasure significantly reduces the 100% accuracy of the Poisoning Prayer to the 40% to 60% range. The study's findings highlight the critical need to address privacy issues in VFL and provide a reference for the development of countermeasures to protect user data confidentiality.

Traditional kernel estimation methods rely on kernel functions, but these functions can be difficult to choose appropriately in certain situations, especially when the underlying data distribution is complex. This study introduces a novel kernel estimator that forgoes the need for kernel functions entirely, instead utilizing the actual data to determine a estimator function through the use of pseudo random fourier features. We establish theoretical performance guarantees for this approach under universal approximation theorems, demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive simulations, and apply this estimator in a genuine dataset analysis.

This research introduces a new technique for mapping complete d-dimensional binary trees onto Cartesian grids without overlap, specifically for even values of d, by converting trees into wreath products using a modified right-hand wall following strategy. A three-dimensional binary tree mapping example is provided to illustrate the technique, followed by the development of a general strategy called the Cartesian partition method for even values of d, consisting of two key components: a group representation into wreath products through semi-direct products and the application of the above-mentioned following strategy, followed by a discussion on the limitations of this method and possible areas for further investigation.

This research focuses on conformally flat hypersurfaces within the sphere $n$-dimensional space, specifically those that do not change under a M\"obius transformation due to their positive curvature. We define a new property called M\"obius scalar curvature stiffness for these hypersurfaces and prove a key characteristic: if the M\"obius remainder term $S$ satisfies $S \le 0$ and is not equal to zero, then the hypersurface is conformally equivalent to the sphere in $n+1$ dimensional space. Additionally, if the M\"obius curvature scalar is constant and positive, then the hypersurface is isometric to the sphere in $n$ dimensional space through a M\"obius transformation.

Two intricate min-max optimization problems are defined to address this issue, which are then resolved using an efficient heuristic method. Furthermore, the SWIPT system model is simplified by comparing it to an alternative model, and the corresponding transmission resource distribution strategies for the simplified model are analyzed.

This research explores an access control problem in multi-user wireless systems with extremely large antennas, where multiple users transmitting to different destinations without any signal interference. The research randomizes visibility graphs representing the areas users can transmit without causing intersections. Given graph data, algorithms are proposed to solve two specific problems: assigning unique transmission channels or transmitting simultaneously on the same channel. Given graph data, probabilistic approaches are used to solve specific problems, including a channel assignment success rate of 84.1% to 94%, and a one-channel transmission success rate ranging from 14.3% to 31.7%. The research also compares performance under varying conditions, changing node transmission ranges, and densities.

Recent observations with the Atacama Cosmology Telescope-2 have revealed puzzling submillimeter substructures in the cosmic microwave background intensity maps. To better understand these substructures, researchers are examining a wider range of candidate lensing sources. We developed a new method to predict the expected dust continuum substructures by utilizing galaxy star formation rate and mass as primary predictors, taking into account environment influences. Our approach, calibrated using data from the SPARC project, results in equations that can be applied to individual galaxies to estimate their submillimeter emission features. When compared to observed data from the ACT and the South Pole Telescope, our predictions provide an accurate representation of the expected features, although discrepancies remain for galaxies with high stellar masses. Our analysis highlights the importance of obtaining spectroscopic observations to accurately measure gas masses and gas-to-stellar mass ratios in a broader range of galaxies, specifically those with higher masses, star formation rates, and lower luminosities.

Recent measurements of the scalar sigma meson mean-field interaction by the STAR collaboration at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider have shown for the first time that sigma mesons significantly influence matter in relativistic heavy ion collisions. By ignoring this interaction, crucial aspects of the phase diagram, results from heavy ion collisions, and the synthesis of neutrons in supernovae and neutron stars could be misinterpreted. A new theoretical model has been developed to accurately account for sigma meson interactions within a wide range of conditions. By eliminating the otherwise repulsive sigma meson interaction below the critical temperature for symmetry breaking, unexpected connections have been discovered. Notably, this phenomenon is linked to the well-known "apple pie theorem" in statistical mechanics and the "big apple strength" in nuclear physics, both suggesting that the heavy ion collisions phase space is filled with vast amounts of sigma mesons that determine the pressure through their number density alone, similar to an ideal gas. As such, these findings call for a reevaluation of our current understanding of hadronic matter generated in heavy ion collisions, the nuclear equation of state, and the formation of neutron stars and supernovae.

Using a mathematical model, we are able to calculate key parameters for the dirac equation that accounts for scattering in various materials. This calculation method is grounded in the perturbation theory and relies on specific assumptions about the scattering potential in the model. As a result, we derived closed-form expressions for key parameters including those related to a gap in the material and the formation of a Landau level in response to the application of a perpendicular magnetic field. By examining a specific type of scattering potential, we calculated parameters for a material known as a "strongly linked" Dirac metal in response to a small applied field that causes a gap in the material's structure and the formation of a specific Landau level when a higher, integer value of a squared, circular shape is created. These calculations are highly relevant to a material known as graphene and other similar materials. Furthermore, the parameters of the material's Hamiltonian in the context of a applied field can be plotted in the form of a phase diagram that outlines the different shapes that can emerge in the material's structure, including a "double gap" and "double mass" when a second, higher, non-zero, and circular shape is created.

Researchers plan to conduct a comprehensive search for charged, neutral, and massive versions of leptons through the analysis of $844$ decays in the NA62 experiment, focusing on the process $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. By this method, they anticipate being able to discover such particles if their mass is between 140 MeV and 1170 MeV, with a signal significance of 3 standard deviations, while the detection threshold varies for different masses, ranging from 5 standard deviations at 145 MeV to 3 standard deviations at 1140 MeV, and can even reach a maximum of 100 standard deviations at lower masses. The proposed analysis strategy relies on the calculation of neutral lepton contributions to decay parameters, and an improved model of photon-induced decays, resulting in an expected collection of over 1.1 billion standard decays with two photons and nearly 550 million decays with only one photon.

Neural text generation methods based on recurrent networks have been outperforming previous $n$-gram language models recently, but during high-resource scenarios where $n$-gram models excel, our research reveals that recurrent networks fail to consistently beat them. We propose a hybrid approach that combines $N$-gram language models with the recurrent components through residual learning, allowing the latter to focus on learning the differences and concentrating on tasks that require complex pattern understanding. Our findings show this combination matches or surpasses the performance of both $N$-gram and recurrent models consistently, and our leading approach even achieves the 17th best result globally in the 9th ICLR text generation challenge by marginally improving the WER metric from 62.6 to 62.5.

Reconstructing the 3D faces of numerous simultaneous faces faces significant challenges due to difficult poses, face-to-face alignment issues, and varied illumination conditions.  Our solution to face reconstruction involves face representation learning from both 2D and 3D info. Our solution to simultaneous face reconstruction is called Self-Aligned Dual Face Prediction Network (SADRNet). In faces with difficult conditions, we use two deep networks to learn face representations from each other, called dual networks, and employ pose, illumination, and occlusion-aligned strategies to predict the remaining info. Our experiment reveals that our method drastically improves face reconstruction, measured by lower NCC and NC values. Our results also show improved accuracy in face landmark prediction, measured by lower values of average point-to-face and eye-to-eye distances. We found that our method yields more precise face landmarks than previous methods, according to MIT-300 and AFD datasets. Our model achieves lower values of average point-to-face and eye-to-eye distances in face landmark prediction, according to MIT-300 and AFD datasets.

We propose an $\alpha$-attractor model featuring a double potential, leading to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). During the early stage, the gradual evolution of the inflaton field precludes the necessary conditions for PBH generation. However, a sudden change (a "kick") in the attractor model's field space introduces a small amplitude of curvature fluctuations. This kick's impact on PBH formation depends on a combination of attractor model parameters and a new input parameter that defines the kick's magnitude. We find that a range of this input parameter allows the conditions for significant PBH generation to be met, given specific choices of model parameters. By integrating the attractor model with a two-field model of massive curvaton inflation following the kick, a detectable level of gravitational waves in the LISA frequency band can be achieved.

Researchers examined the properties of labeled ordered trees, focusing on the different categories of vertices based on the depth at which they appear. They analyzed four specific categories: the maximum depth at which vertices can appear, the easiest depth at which vertices can appear, the deepest depth at which vertices can appear, and the minimum depth at which vertices can appear. By establishing the unique distribution rules for each category, they developed distinct approaches to calculate the number of labeled ordered trees that contain at least one vertex from each depth category. Additionally, they derived formulas for calculating the number of labeled ordered trees that can accommodate vertices at a specified set of depths.

Election results depend on accurate data processing, including aggregating raw vote counts from various candidates and parties. To ensure accurate data aggregation, different jurisdictions need reliable tools to process and sum vote counts from election forms. This process is complicated by the diverse formats used in different jurisdictions, making manual verification time-consuming and prone to errors. While automated systems like OCR exist to process these forms, they lack uniformity in accuracy due to the varied formats used across jurisdictions. To address this challenge, we developed iOCR, an adaptive Informed Optical Symbol Recognition system that adjusts its processing based on the format of the jurisdiction's form. iOCR uses basic information to identify the format and then employs tailored regression models to estimate the values of unknown symbols. This system combines low-data models with human annotations to minimize errors. Our evaluation of iOCR across 20 jurisdictions demonstrates its reliability, with a 99.2% accuracy rate in testing data, allowing for efficient post-election oversight and analysis.

In scenarios where data points represent time-series data in a linear model with additional parameters, research indicates that models lacking inherent sparsity assumptions can effectively utilize the temporal relationships between data points for prediction, provided the error distribution follows a Gaussian norm. This study delves into the theoretical foundations of benign overfitting in a linear regression model with temporal parameterization and error, demonstrating that a specific variant of Recurrent Least Squares (RLS) algorithm accomplishes a test loss bound of $\tau_{\text{test}} \approx \sigma_s^2 + s \cdot \sigma_\epsilon \sqrt{\frac{\log d}{n}}$ under certain conditions, where $\log d$ is constrained by the effective degree of freedom of RLS threshold within the training dataset. RLS achieves sparse modeling through regularization, incorporating $N$ observations and $d$ features with $N$ and $d$ being equivalent to the number of RLS parameters in the training data. Our findings are further validated through numerical experiments.

In this study, a cautious storage planning approach is proposed for decentralized energy markets to prevent unnecessary storage investments caused by overly optimistic market projections.  Rather than adopting multiple independent forecasts, the agent utilizes the cautious self-constructive prediction (cscp) method to create robust supply storage investment plans.  By incorporating risk aversion and assuming the worst-case scenario within a defined set of possible predictions, cscp ensures robust and reliable outcomes.  Numerical results based on an AC-DC test system under various prediction sets and risk aversion levels, demonstrate the effectiveness of the cautious self-constructive storage planning in achieving reliable, risk-aware decision-making under uncertainty.

A computational experiment on a 2D Earth atmosphere model in a comparative cyclostrophic and geostrophic land circulation regimes on terrestrial rocks shows that gravity-driven currents around hot and cool regions lead to significant heating by frictional effects when temperatures rise near the stars and cool by radiation at higher distances from the stars.

Overcoming the static nature of modern neural network implementations, which typically involve pre-trained models that serve as fixed predictors or require full re-training when objectives change, dynamic learning enables the creation of adaptable systems that can modify their structure and parameters in real-time to adapt to new tasks. While previous research has explored this concept primarily with simple neural network models using vast amounts of data and computational power, we investigate the feasibility of applying dynamic learning to modify the parameters and structure of a state-of-the-art vision transformer (ViT) model on an extensive dataset comprising 14.2 million images. Our approach successfully demonstrates that a single, initially uniform ViT can be divided into multiple specialized sub-networks that serve as effective predictors for distinct classes of data, and we explore various learning strategies to create these specialists, including methods that result in highly performant specialized sub-networks and a single, unified model that can generalize to unknown tasks.

Silicon-based quantum dots are highly suitable for implementing entangled states, a critical requirement for performing complex, sequential operations. Researchers have explored various configurations of donor-based spin systems involving both nuclear and electronic multi-valley states within the valence band. However, an obstacle arises due to the inherent coupling of states within the two valleys through the exchange interaction, which necessitates precise measurements of exchange interactions among the valence states to address the ci problem within multi-valley systems through conventional molecular field approximation or density functional theory. Utilizing the multi-valley effective mass model, which bypasses integration over spatial coordinates, we obtained a breakthrough in obtaining a first-principles solution to the exchange interaction problem of nuclear and electronic spin systems by developing a CI solver for the multi-valley model. We found that exchange interactions primarily influence the total electron nuclear state's phase without influencing the magnitude, a finding that aligns with results from previous studies employing non-effective model approaches. As such, most existing methods for resolving the ci problem within multi-valley systems can be directly applied to address this problem.

We investigated the transport properties of mercury telluride (HgTe) quantum well structures situated on both mercury telluride cadmium telluride (HgTe/CdTe) and mercury telluride beryllium telluride (HgTe/BeTe) quantum plates, specifically where the particle-hole symmetry remains intact and is broken. 
Our theoretical approach utilized the Landau-Bethe-Salpeter equation to determine the filling factors within these structures, and found that near the center of the spectrum, there's robust conductance quantization corresponding to filled negative helicity states. 
By altering the well's thickness, we observed that increased telluride welling leads to states with opposite helicity being filled, resulting in a shift in conductance by $2e^2/h$. 
This finding aligns with experimental observations where state helicity is influenced by the energy levels of heavy and light holes, and leads to a specific sequence of conductance values as the well's thickness increases. 
However, when particle-hole symmetry is disrupted, we predicted that the conduction shifts by $e^2/h$ for each welling state that mixes with the conduction band, specifically $\nu = -6 \times (N_h - N_v)$ for HgTe quantum wells with HgTe/CdTe barriers and $\nu = -4 \times (N_h - N_v)$ for HgTe quantum wells with BeTe barriers.

Imbalanced uplink and downlink traffic patterns in radio access networks due to fixed time-synchronization protocols in TDD systems can lead to inefficient data transmission. To mitigate this issue, self-organizing networks (SON) have been employed to dynamically adjust uplink and downlink configurations to optimize scheduling protocols. Non-cooperative nature of cellular base stations necessitates the use of game theory to devise a novel downlink configuration selection method that maximizes each base station's utility without considering overall system utility. A proposed Stackelberg leader-follower game enables the main base station to set an initial configuration, which subsequent base stations can either adhere to or adjust based on their specific cell conditions. Despite its effectiveness, the proposed solution requires considerable computational resources, prompting the development of a simplified two-player game that allows base stations to make informed decisions with limited processing power, crucial for 5G deployments. Evaluation results demonstrate the proposed two-player game's ability to significantly enhance scheduling efficiency, achieve a substantial improvement in overall system utility, and minimize configuration changes across the network, crucial for maintaining network stability in 5G deployments.

In this work, we highlight the limitations of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) when using standard loss functions that drive the difference between predicted and actual predicted momenta and velocities. We HNNs demonstrate that the model often struggles to capture variations in important variables due to an excessive smoothing effect induced by this approach. Furthermore, we introduce an novel inference mechanism for differentiable neural models, specifically targeting such smoothness barriers. Leveraging this technique, we modify HNNs to differentiate gradients effectively. Our approach yields more controlled and informative model visualizations, thus demonstrating the feasibility of purposeful model styling in neural Hamiltonians.

The rapid advancement of machine learning technologies has given rise to powerful models such as large language models, which are increasingly utilized in various applications. Despite their capabilities, there's a concern that users may place too much trust in these models, potentially leading to significant consequences. This study introduces a novel multi-agent framework for assessing user trust in AI models, incorporating a human-in-the-loop approach. This involves combining the input of individual users, specifically through the collection of feedback and ratings regarding their confidence in the model's predictions, along with synthetic data generated to enhance efficiency. This method utilizes a human-generated labeling space, categorizing labels into precise, broad, and distorted classifications, and assigns ratings that reflect the level of accuracy required for each classification. This study employs a modified importance sampling technique, incorporating a weight function to adjust for the addition of synthetic data, ensuring that the resulting dataset remains representative while giving greater emphasis to certain categories of feedback, particularly those with higher accuracy requirements. Through numerical experiments, this approach demonstrates improved generalization performance compared to traditional retraining methods, effectively balancing user trust in models with their performance.
